questions.question: What are the @Transactional propagation types and when would you use each?
questions.title: @Transactional — Propagation Types
questions.direct_answer: **`@Transactional` propagation** controls how a method behaves when a transaction already exists. **`REQUIRED`** (the default) joins an existing transaction or creates one — failure rolls back the entire outer transaction. **`REQUIRES_NEW`** suspends the existing transaction and creates an independent one on a separate connection — use it for audit logs and notifications that must persist regardless of business outcome. **`NESTED`** uses a savepoint within the same connection — inner failure can be caught while outer continues. **`MANDATORY`**, **`NEVER`**, **`NOT_SUPPORTED`**, and **`SUPPORTS`** cover specialized scenarios where you want to assert or change the transactional context without creating a new one.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to reason about transaction boundaries and choose the right propagation for audit logs, batch jobs, or compensating transactions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using REQUIRED everywhere without understanding that an exception in a nested REQUIRED call will roll back the entire outer transaction.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain NESTED (uses a savepoint so the inner work can be rolled back independently while the outer transaction commits) and contrast it with REQUIRES_NEW (fully separate transaction, separate connection).

sections.title: Why REQUIRED Is the Default — and Why It Causes the Most Subtle Bugs
sections.content:
**Propagation defines how the transactional context is shared** between caller and callee. Getting this wrong is a common source of data-consistency bugs — either over-sharing a transaction so an unrelated failure causes a global rollback, or creating too many independent transactions and losing atomicity.

`@Transactional` propagation types control what happens when a transactional method calls another transactional method. **The seven propagation levels** handle three key scenarios: whether to **join** an existing transaction, **create a new one**, or **refuse to participate**.

The most important distinction in practice is **`REQUIRED` rolls back together**. If an inner `REQUIRED` method throws, the entire outer transaction rolls back. Developers who add an audit log call inside a business transaction and use `REQUIRED` find their audit log disappears whenever the business transaction fails. The fix is `REQUIRES_NEW`.

sections.title: The Seven Propagation Types — What Each One Does
sections.content:
Each propagation type answers a single question: **what should happen to the transaction context when this method is called?**

**`REQUIRED` (default)**
- Join the existing transaction if one exists; otherwise create a new one
- Correct for most service methods
- If the inner method throws, the entire transaction rolls back — both methods share the same physical transaction

**`REQUIRES_NEW`**
- Always create a new physical transaction, suspending the outer one
- Inner transaction commits or rolls back independently on a separate connection
- Use for operations that must succeed regardless of the outer transaction's outcome — audit logging, notification sending, idempotency token recording

**`NESTED`**
- Create a savepoint within the existing transaction
- If the inner method fails, only the work since the savepoint is rolled back
- The outer transaction can catch the exception and continue
- Requires JDBC savepoint support; not supported by all JPA providers

**`SUPPORTS`**
- Run in the existing transaction if one exists; otherwise run non-transactionally
- Useful for read methods that benefit from transaction consistency when called from a transactional context but work fine without one

**`MANDATORY`**
- Requires an existing transaction; throws `IllegalTransactionStateException` if none exists
- Enforces that a method is never called standalone — must always be part of a larger unit of work

**`NOT_SUPPORTED`**
- Suspend any existing transaction and run non-transactionally
- Useful for cache warmup, external API calls that should not participate in the caller's transaction

**`NEVER`**
- Throw an exception if a transaction exists
- Inverse of `MANDATORY` — enforces that the method is never called within a transaction context

sections.title: All Seven Propagation Types — Decision at a Glance
sections.content:
The seven propagation types differ in what they do when called with or without an existing transaction. The table below makes the decision visible in one view.

| Propagation | Existing Tx | Behavior | Classic Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REQUIRED` (default) | Yes | Join it | Service layer methods |
| `REQUIRED` | No | Create new | Service layer methods |
| `REQUIRES_NEW` | Yes | Suspend + create new | Audit logging, notifications |
| `REQUIRES_NEW` | No | Create new | Audit logging, notifications |
| `NESTED` | Yes | Savepoint + continue | Optional sub-operations in batch |
| `NESTED` | No | Create new | Optional sub-operations |
| `SUPPORTS` | Yes | Join it | Read-only reporting queries |
| `SUPPORTS` | No | Run non-transactionally | Read-only reporting queries |
| `NOT_SUPPORTED` | Yes | Suspend + run non-tx | Legacy code, long-running reports |
| `MANDATORY` | Yes | Join it | Internal methods always called within tx |
| `MANDATORY` | No | Throw exception | Internal methods always called within tx |
| `NEVER` | Yes | Throw exception | Batch exports that must not hold locks |
| `NEVER` | No | Run non-transactionally | Batch exports |

The high-frequency mistake: using `REQUIRED` for an audit log inside a business transaction. When the business transaction fails, the audit log disappears with it. The fix is `REQUIRES_NEW`.

sections.title: REQUIRES_NEW vs NESTED — Two Isolation Mechanisms
sections.content:
`REQUIRES_NEW` and `NESTED` both provide rollback isolation from the outer transaction, but they work through fundamentally different mechanisms with different failure characteristics.

**`REQUIRES_NEW` — separate connection**
- Suspends the outer transaction entirely
- Opens a new database connection (or borrows from the pool)
- Inner transaction commits or rolls back on its own connection
- If the inner transaction commits before the outer fails, the inner commit is **permanent** — the database cannot undo it when the outer transaction rolls back on a different connection
- Exactly what audit logging needs: the log entry persists even if the business operation fails

**`NESTED` — savepoint on same connection**
- Uses a savepoint within the same physical connection
- When the inner method begins, Spring (via JDBC) issues `SAVEPOINT inner_tx`
- If the inner method throws, Spring rolls back to the savepoint — undoing only the inner work
- The outer transaction can catch the exception and continue
- If the outer transaction fails, the rollback undoes everything back to the start — including work done within the nested transaction, since it's all on the same connection

**Code example**

```java
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
public void writeAuditLog(AuditEntry entry) {
    auditRepo.save(entry);
}

@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.NESTED)
public void enrichWithExternalData(Order order) {
    ExternalData data = externalApiClient.fetch(order.getId());
    order.setExternalMetadata(data);
}
```

**The resource cost of `REQUIRES_NEW`**
- Each `REQUIRES_NEW` call borrows a connection from the pool for the duration of the inner transaction
- The outer transaction still holds its connection
- For a service that processes 100 requests/sec with 5 `REQUIRES_NEW` audit calls each, you're using 6× the connections you'd expect
- **Connection pool exhaustion under load is the failure mode**
- `NESTED` avoids this: one connection, one transaction, multiple savepoints

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`REQUIRED` rolls back together** — an exception in an inner `REQUIRED` call rolls back the entire outer transaction; an audit log inside a `REQUIRED` call disappears if the business transaction fails.
- **`REQUIRES_NEW` uses a separate physical connection** — suspends the outer transaction and borrows a new connection from the pool; the inner commit is permanent even if the outer transaction later rolls back; doubles connection usage under load.
- **`NESTED` uses a savepoint on the same connection** — inner failure rolls back to the savepoint; outer can catch and continue; outer failure rolls back everything including the nested work.
- **Self-invocation bypasses `@Transactional` entirely** — regardless of propagation type, calling a `@Transactional` method via `this` goes through the original object, not the proxy; no transaction management.
- **`REQUIRES_NEW` connection exhaustion at scale** — each `REQUIRES_NEW` call borrows a connection while the outer still holds one; in a high-throughput service with multiple audit calls per request, connection pool exhaustion becomes the failure mode.
- **`NESTED` requires JDBC savepoint support** — works with most relational databases but not with all JPA providers; check `JpaTransactionManager` documentation for compatibility.
- **`MANDATORY` and `NEVER` enforce contracts** — use `MANDATORY` to assert that internal methods are only called within an existing transaction; use `NEVER` to ensure batch exports don't hold locks.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@Transactional` propagation controls what happens to the transaction context when one transactional method calls another. Getting it wrong produces data-consistency bugs — audit logs that vanish, operations that should be independent sharing a rollback boundary.

**`REQUIRED` (the default)**
- Joins the existing transaction if one is active; creates a new one if not
- Inner and outer method share the same physical transaction — an exception anywhere rolls back everything
- The audit log trap: write an audit log inside a `REQUIRED` call and the outer transaction fails — the audit log disappears with it

**`REQUIRES_NEW`**
- Always creates a new, independent transaction, suspending the outer one
- Uses a separate database connection — the inner commit is permanent even if the outer transaction later rolls back
- The right choice for audit logging and notifications that must persist regardless of the business outcome
- The cost: two open connections simultaneously; under high load with many `REQUIRES_NEW` calls per request, connection pool exhaustion becomes the failure mode

**`NESTED`**
- Creates a savepoint within the same physical connection
- Inner failure rolls back to the savepoint; the outer transaction can catch the exception and continue
- Outer failure rolls back everything — all work on the same connection
- Lower resource cost than `REQUIRES_NEW` but requires JDBC savepoint support

Regardless of propagation type: calling a `@Transactional` method via `this` bypasses the proxy — no transaction management at all. The propagation setting has no effect on self-invocation.

questions.question: How do Spring profiles work? Explain @Profile and spring.profiles.active.
questions.title: Spring Profiles (@Profile, spring.profiles.active)
questions.direct_answer: **Spring profiles** let you register beans and load configuration conditionally based on the active environment (dev, staging, prod, test). A bean annotated with **`@Profile("prod")`** is only created when the `prod` profile is active. Profiles are activated via **`spring.profiles.active`** in `application.properties`, an environment variable (`SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`), a JVM/CLI argument (`--spring.profiles.active=prod`), or programmatically. Multiple profiles can be active simultaneously. Spring Boot also loads **profile-specific property files** (`application-{profile}.yml`) automatically, and **profile groups** (Spring Boot 2.4+) let you activate a composite profile with one name.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical ability to configure environment-specific beans (datasources, mocks, feature flags) and understanding of profile inheritance.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Hardcoding environment-specific values in beans instead of using profiles, or not knowing that multiple profiles can be active simultaneously.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain profile groups (spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring) introduced in Spring Boot 2.4, and the difference between default profile and fallback profile behavior.

sections.title: Why Profiles Exist — Environment-Specific Configuration Without Code Changes
sections.content:
**Profiles provide a first-class mechanism** for separating environment-specific configuration.
- Rather than using if/else logic or property placeholders throughout your beans, you declare entire bean graphs that are only wired in specific environments.
- Spring Boot extends this to property files (`application-prod.properties`) and profile groups.

**The same JAR behaves differently** in dev, staging, and production based on which profiles are active. This is the core deployment principle that makes immutable artifacts possible — one binary, many environments.

**Profiles are also test infrastructure**. `@ActiveProfiles("test")` on integration test classes loads `application-test.yml` with in-memory databases, mock service URLs, and debug logging. This isolation ensures tests never accidentally hit production resources.

sections.title: Step 1 — Define Profile-Specific Beans
Step 2 — Activate Profiles (Priority Order Matters)
sections.content:
Spring profiles can be activated through multiple mechanisms. They follow a **priority order** that matters when the same property is set in different places — the highest-priority source wins.

**Command-line arguments — highest priority**
- `--spring.profiles.active=prod` overrides everything else
- Standard for containerized deployments where the orchestrator (Kubernetes, ECS) passes config at launch

**Environment variables — second priority**
- `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod`
- The Docker-friendly approach — set in the Dockerfile or container spec

**`application.properties` — lowest priority**
- `spring.profiles.active=dev`
- Typically the developer default — local development runs with `dev` unless overridden

**Programmatic activation**
- `SpringApplication.setAdditionalProfiles("prod")` before `app.run(args)`
- Useful for embedded scenarios where the activation logic is dynamic

**Test activation**
- `@ActiveProfiles("test")` on test classes — activates the test profile for that test

```properties
# application.properties
spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring
```

```bash
-Dspring.profiles.active=prod
export SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
```

```java
SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(App.class);
app.setAdditionalProfiles("prod");
app.run(args);

@SpringBootTest
@ActiveProfiles("test")
class OrderServiceTest { ... }
```

**Multiple profiles active simultaneously**
- `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring` activates both
- Beans annotated with either `@Profile("prod")` or `@Profile("monitoring")` will be registered

sections.title: Step 3 — Profile-Specific Property Files
sections.content:
**Beyond beans**, profiles control which property files Spring loads. The naming convention is `application-{profile}.properties` (or `.yml`).

**Loading rules**
- Base file `application.properties` is always loaded
- Profile-specific file `application-{profile}.properties` is loaded when that profile is active
- **Profile-specific properties take precedence** over base properties for any key present in both

**Common pattern — vary by environment**

```properties
app.cache.ttl=60s
logging.level.root=INFO

logging.level.root=DEBUG
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

app.cache.ttl=3600s
logging.level.root=WARN
```

**The base file defines defaults**; the profile file overrides what's different. This is how you vary database URLs, logging levels, and feature flags without touching code.

**Common security mistake**
- Putting production secrets directly in `application-prod.properties` and committing them to version control
- Profile-specific files should contain non-sensitive overrides only
- Secrets belong in environment variables, Vault, or AWS Secrets Manager — injected at runtime, never stored in the repository

sections.title: Step 4 — Profile Groups (Spring Boot 2.4+)
sections.content:
**Spring Boot 2.4 introduced profile groups**, which solve the problem of activating multiple related profiles together.

**The problem before groups**
- Deploying to production meant setting `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring,security`
- A list that grows with every new concern
- Easy to get wrong; every deployment script needed to know all the sub-profiles

**Groups solution**
- Define composite profiles in `application.properties`
- Activate just the group name and all member profiles activate automatically

```properties
spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring,security-hardened
spring.profiles.group.local=dev,mockservices

spring.profiles.active=production
```

**Equivalent to**: `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring,security-hardened`

**Benefits**
- Keeps environment configuration manageable as the number of concerns grows
- Adding a new monitoring profile means editing the group definition in one place, not updating every deployment pipeline
- Deployment scripts activate a single semantic group, not a long comma-separated list

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Profile("!prod")` registers in all profiles except production** — negation syntax enables beans that exist in every environment except one; common for debug tooling and test data seeders.
- **Multiple profiles can be active simultaneously** — `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring` activates both; beans annotated with either profile are registered.
- **Profile-specific property files override the base** — `application-prod.properties` overrides `application.properties` for any key present in both; the base file provides defaults.
- **Profile groups (Spring Boot 2.4+)** — `spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring,security` lets you activate a composite with a single name; keeps deployment scripts from growing long profile lists.
- **Activation priority: command-line > env var > `application.properties`** — `--spring.profiles.active=prod` on the command line overrides `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE` env var, which overrides the property file.
- **`@ActiveProfiles("test")` in tests** — activates the `test` profile for `@SpringBootTest`, loading `application-test.properties` with H2, mock service URLs, and debug logging.
- **Profiles enable immutable artifacts** — the same JAR runs in every environment; profile activation at launch determines configuration.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring profiles let you register different bean graphs and load different property files based on the active environment — without changing code or rebuilding the artifact. The same JAR behaves differently in dev, staging, and production based on which profiles are active.

**Profile-specific beans**
- `@Profile("prod")` on a `@Bean` or `@Configuration` class — only registered when `prod` is active
- `@Profile("!prod")` — registered in every profile except production; common for debug tooling and mock services
- Multiple active profiles at once: `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring` — beans from both profiles are registered

**Activating profiles — priority order**
- Command-line `--spring.profiles.active=prod` — highest priority, overrides everything else
- Environment variable `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` — Docker and Kubernetes standard
- `spring.profiles.active=dev` in `application.properties` — developer default, lowest priority

**Profile-specific property files**
- `application-prod.properties` loads automatically when `prod` is active and overrides the base `application.properties` for any key present in both
- Base file sets defaults; profile files override what is environment-specific

**Profile groups (Spring Boot 2.4+)**
- `spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring,security` — activate `production` and all three sub-profiles activate automatically

In tests, `@ActiveProfiles("test")` loads `application-test.properties` — typically with an H2 in-memory database, mock service URLs, and verbose logging. Tests never accidentally hit production resources.
